newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-INCO to maintain leading position.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-INCO to maintain leading position.

text.p: Canadian nickel giant Inco Ltd intends to maintain its position as the world's leading nickel producer - a role that will be strengthened by its Voisey's Bay project, Inco President Scott M. Hand said.

"Inco's strategy is to be the world's leadest nickel producer, you have to grow, you have to be low cost...With Voisey's Bay our nickel production will grow by over 80 percent," Hand said in an interview.
Inco is currently working to receieve the required approvals in order to start construction at the resource in Labrador that Inco purchased in 1996 from Diamond Fields.
"The time schedule has not changed...We would hope that we could get the first concentrate out in Labrador by the end of 1999 and have a smelter and refinery up and running by 2000," Hand said.
As of yet there are many issues to be agreed regarding the environmental review, talks with aboriginal groups, and the tax regime.
There are also discussions between the provincial authorities and the federal government over land claims, which Inco is not involved in.
Meanwhile, Inco continues to explore and test drill at the property, and is confident that the project and the resource will continue to grow.
Recent drilling in what is known as the Western extension have intersected high grade material similar to the Ovoid (the original resource).
"When it somes into production it (Voisey's Bay) will produce around 270 million lbs of nickel, around 200 million lbs of copper and six million lbs of cobalt (annually)," Hand said.
"Because the initial seven years will be open-pit operations, costs will be low so there will be substantial cash flows generated, he added.
Inco's current cash/costs are $1.54/lb, but when Voisey's Bay comes onstream they will fall to $1.18, a percentage cost cut of 23 percent.
This is based on $0.80/lb for copper and $10/lb for cobalt.
"If prices of copper and cobalt are higher then that minus 23 percent will be more," he added.
As well as Voisey's Bay, Inco has expansion plans at PT Inco in Indonesia and an undeveloped project at Goro in New Caledonia.
Inco also spends considerable sums of money on product research in speciality nickel products, such as nickel-cadmium and nickel-hydride batteries.
"Our sales of nickel powders and other forms are growing every year. We are a producer of high-tech speciality products," Hand said.
Technological developments are also being utilised in order to keep costs competitive, as the strongest producers are the lowest cost producers.
At Goro Inco is piloting a new hydrometallurgical process, and in Canada there are moves towards robotic mining operations, he said.

At Stobie in Ontario, robotic scoops and drills are already in operation, which offer significant potential for increased productivity. Inco is also working with a number of other companies in explosives and mining equipment to develop a robotic mine.

"That mine will be operated from the surface. We are putting a lot of money into that as we see it as a way of getting a quantum reduction in costs and increase in productivity. Importantly, it will also be a safer mine," Hand said.
